concepts.concept_description: Adding and utilizing the Video Sensing extension in Scratch to interact with a live camera feed.
Using the 'turn video on' block to activate the webcam within a Scratch project, typically triggered by an event like 'when green flag clicked'.
Using the 'set video transparency to' block to control how visible the live video feed is on the stage. A value of 0 makes it fully opaque.
Creating several different costumes for a single sprite using the built-in paint editor to represent various face filters like hats, glasses, and mustaches.
Using the 'next costume' block to cycle through a sprite's available costumes in sequence.
Using the 'when this sprite clicked' event block to trigger an action, such as changing to the next costume, when the user clicks on the sprite.
Using a 'forever' loop to make a set of commands run continuously throughout the project's execution, such as constantly checking for video motion.
Using the 'wait until' block to pause a script's execution until a specific Boolean condition becomes true, such as waiting for video motion to exceed a certain threshold.
Using the 'video motion on sprite' reporter block from the Video Sensing extension to measure the amount of motion detected over a sprite.
Using a comparison operator (e.g., '>') to compare a sensor value ('video motion') with a constant number (e.g., 50) to create a conditional statement.
Designing a program that waits for and reacts to a real-world event (user motion detected by the camera) to trigger a specific action (changing a costume).
Utilizing the tools within the Scratch Paint Editor (like Fill, Outline, Brush) to draw custom graphics for sprite costumes.
Using the 'wait <> seconds' block to create a timed delay in a script, for example, to pause for a few seconds before changing to the next filter.
Setting up the initial state of the program when the green flag is clicked, such as turning on the video and setting its transparency.
